This portion of the Turkish capital received the name Galata about the 9th century.

After the restoration of the Byzantine Empire, in 1267 A. D., the Genoese residents of Constantinople were removed to Galata by Emperor Michael Paleologus. The colony was practically independent, having its own laws and government administered by a Podesta. However, after the capture of Constantinople in 1453 by the Turks, Muhammed II, put an end to the independence of the Galata Genoese, notwithstanding the fact that they had assisted him in the siege in the hopes that their charter might be renewed.

Galata has a fine location, being built upon a slope of ground that forms a promontory between the Golden Horn and the Bosphorus. In its foreground is the beautiful Golden Horn, on the opposite shore of which lies the picturesque Moslem city, Stamboul. Galata and Pera form the European section of Constantinople, Galata being the center of business enterprise while Pera, situated at a higher point on the elevation, forms the residence quarter. Like all Constantinople, Galata has a much more attractive appearance from a distance, for when in contact with its narrow and dirty streets the charm is somewhat dispelled.
